doc.title: Milt Fillius interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 18, 2000

title: Desert island recordings and the Four Brothers bet
summary: Choices include Goodman, Basie, Joe Williams, Woody Herman and Ellington, with a bet won and a Paul Gonsalves story.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: But if you had to pick out three or four recordings that you would have on that proverbial desert island with you, the only thing that you had to listen to, can you think of a couple of things that for you really personify what the music was about? I know you’ve had so many, I’ve been moving your records around.

“Swingtime in the Rockies,” Benny Goodman. I’d take several Basie tunes. There’s so many of them I can’t think really. I think the Hefti stuff is very good. I’d take Joe Williams’ “Our Love is Here to Stay.” I’d take “Four Brothers,” from Woody Herman. I won a big bet with that one day by the way.

Yeah we hired a new agency, an ad agency, and we got to talking about jazz, and I said I know a lot of jazz guys and so on and so forth. The guy says well I’ll put you to the test. So he brought in the record the “Four Brothers.” And they set it up in the room next door a couple of weeks later. And he brought me in and said, “Now what is this?” I says, “That’s the ‘Four Brothers,’” and then I named the four sax players. He died. He died. Well that’s a sterling tune. That’s really good. Ellington — I’d take a medley of all his stuff which he always does on his concerts, and I’d take the “Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue” for the tremendous sax part, that’s Paul Gonsalves. Incidentally I saw them once, I think it was at Monterey. They had an intermission and Paul came back and he © Fillius Jazz Archive -22-

was stoned. Either drunk or out on dope or something, and he came back and he sat there at the stand, just out of it. Everybody’s playing the set, and they started the “Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue” and they got to the sax solo, all of a sudden he came to, he stood up and he played his brains out. Amazing.
